values.value: MCP: The USB-C Port for AI
Before MCP, every AI integration was a bespoke cable. The Model Context Protocol gives assistants one standard plug for every tool, and that changes everything.

value.markup:
Remember the drawer full of chargers? Every phone, camera and gadget had its own plug, and you needed the right cable for each one. Until recently, connecting AI assistants to real tools felt the same: every integration was a one-off, hand-wired to a single model and a single API.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the USB-C moment for AI. It is an open standard that describes how an assistant discovers tools, calls them and gets structured results back. Build an MCP server once, and any MCP-capable client can use it.

values.value: One protocol, many connections. Photo by Alina Grubnyak on Unsplash
Write the integration once, and every MCP-capable assistant can use it.
The promise of the Model Context Protocol

value.markup:
Why a standard beats a pile of plugins

Standards compound. When tool builders and assistant builders agree on one protocol, each side only has to do its half of the work once. A CMS vendor ships an MCP server, and it immediately works in desktop assistants, IDEs, terminals and custom agents.

  • Discovery: tools describe themselves, so the assistant knows what it can do and what inputs each tool expects.
  • Safety: the server decides what is exposed, and clients can ask a human before anything destructive runs.
  • Portability: switch models or clients without rewriting your integrations.

That is why MCP is awesome: it turns AI integrations from craft projects into infrastructure.

values.value: Why MCP Makes Your CMS Smarter
Give an AI assistant real tools instead of copy-paste, and it stops guessing about your content model. Here is what that looks like in Umbraco.

value.markup:
Ask a chatbot to help with your website and it will happily invent document types, property aliases and APIs that do not exist. It is not being careless; it simply cannot see your system. All it has is what you paste into the chat.

MCP changes that. With an Umbraco MCP server connected, the assistant can look before it acts: list your document types, read a page, inspect its blocks and check which data types already exist. The guessing stops because the facts are one tool call away.

values.value: The best way to stop an assistant from hallucinating your content model is to let it read your content model.
Every developer who has tried it
The pieces finally fit. Photo by Vardan Papikyan on Unsplash

value.markup:
Two servers, two jobs

This very site was built with two MCP servers side by side. The developer server shapes the schema: element types, a block grid data type, page types, templates and media. The editor server handles content: creating pages, adding blocks and publishing.

Splitting the work this way mirrors how real teams operate. Developers own the structure, editors own the words, and the assistant can switch hats without ever reaching around the CMS into the database.

The result is an assistant that works with Umbraco's conventions instead of against them. That is the real superpower of MCP: not doing more, but doing it the right way.
